q: When conversational history enters memory, should the basic retained object be raw turns, fixed chunks, topic-bounded episodes, extracted facts, or some combination?
a: Retain topic-bounded episode summaries plus exhaustive transient semantics, then derive user experience traces.

q: When should a new episode begin: at every session boundary, at fixed size, or when a model infers a topic change using surrounding context?
a: Classify every utterance as topic change or topic development using preceding and subsequent context; contiguous same-topic utterances form an episode.

q: When an utterance contains text and visual context, how much should semantic extraction preserve versus discard?
a: Extract an “exhaustive” fact-based semantic representation, including image details, names, colors, and descriptors, using the current utterance plus two prior utterances and image metadata.

q: When dialogue concerns several people, whose experience should be converted into durable personal memory?
a: Build a separate trace/card for each participant; facts about another person are retained in that person’s own trace, even if mentioned during someone else’s topic.

q: Which candidate facts deserve durable retention: all personal experiences, only concrete biographical facts, only user-confirmed facts, or only task-relevant durable facts?
a: A prompt rule retains concrete biographical facts and contextual details about the subject’s own life; acknowledgements and social pleasantries are filtered.

q: When information is filtered out, should the system delete it silently, preserve it as an episode, log the rejection, or expose the reason?
a: Trace distillation can return N/A; episode summaries remain. The paper reports aggregate “discard rate,” but per-item reason logging and user exposure are underspecified.

q: Should a memory distinguish what the user stated from what the system observed or hypothesized?
a: No explicit epistemic tier is stored. Concrete experiences are distilled and summarized into narrative threads; the schema carries hierarchy, summaries, and IDs, not stated/observed/hypothesized status.

q: When many traces accumulate, should organization be chronological, graph-based, schema-based, or discovered through semantic clustering?
a: Use PCA → UMAP → HDBSCAN; reassign all noise with KNN; cluster first into topics and then into fine-grained, chronologically sequential threads.

q: When a trace is an outlier, should it remain noise, be discarded, or be forced into the nearest narrative?
a: HDBSCAN flags noise; KNN then assigns every noise point to the nearest coherent cluster.

q: What should the long-term user model expose to retrieval: atomic claims, a graph, chronological episodes, or a summarized narrative hierarchy?
a: A three-level memory card: overall theme → topic → thread title/summary/ID, with thread content separately retrievable.

q: At query time, should retrieval use one index or combine direct episodic similarity with navigation through a user-level schema?
a: In parallel, retrieve top-10 episodic memories by vector similarity and use an LLM to select card(s) and up to 10 threads per person; fuse both

q: What should select the relevant person-level memory: explicit identity, query cues inferred by a model, authorization scope, or all available cards?
a: An LLM chooses one or both user cards from query cues; it must select at least one.

q: When memory exists but the interaction contract does not call for it, should the system still retrieve it, suppress retrieval, or retrieve and gate disclosure?
a: Implemented system retrieves for answering; when not to invoke memory is deferred as future work. No disclosure policy is specified.

q: When retrieved evidence is missing, ambiguous, or contradictory, should the system abstain, ask, expose uncertainty, or guess?
a: The answer prompt says that if evidence is unavailable, “try your best guess.” Conflict resolution is underspecified.

q: When newer information conflicts with an older memory, should both remain, should one supersede the other, or should the system reconcile them into a revised claim?
a: Underspecified. Chronological threads retain sequences, but there is no operational contradiction, supersession, correction, or version policy.

q: What should change over time: cluster organization, claim validity, confidence, retention, or all of them?
a: The paper calls cards “self-evolving,” apparently through consolidation/reorganization; retrieval-triggered rewriting, decay, and regulated forgetting are only proposed future directions.

q: What provenance should survive compression, and who should be able to inspect it?
a: Thread IDs link card summaries back to thread contents; episodic memories and threads feed the answer. Claim-to-source granularity and a user-facing provenance interface are underspecified.

q: What happens when the memory system is wrong: automatic rewrite, silent persistence, user correction, rollback, or deletion?
a: Underspecified. No correction, edit, removal, appeal, or rollback surface is described; rewriting on retrieval is future speculation.

q: Should generation receive all retrieved content, a reranked subset, or a permission-filtered trace with reasons?
a: Fuse top episodic memories and selected thread contents into the answering context. Reranking, token budgeting, deduplication, and conflict ordering are underspecified.

q: What should the user see of memory operation: only the final answer, citations, the retrieved memories, withheld memories, or the whole editable model?
a: The paper specifies answer generation, not a user-facing memory or explanation surface; exposure is underspecified.
